item.title: Nobody wants your AI app
item.description: The switchboard operator’s job was automated out of existence. The work it became, the invisible systems that now connect every call, is worth more than the job ever was. AI is about to do the same thing to the app.The people buying AI are blunt about the fact that the future is intelligence that disappears into existing platforms. Everyone wants it invisible and under their total control at the same time.We are all racing to build AI apps that nobody wants to open.Specifically, the standalone AI app, the thing you download, log into, and go to, is a worse idea than almost anyone building in the space wants to admit.The numbers are brutal. According to RevenueCat’s analysis of more than 115,000 apps, AI apps are fantastic at getting you to sign up and terrible at getting you to stay. They convert free users to paid faster than regular apps, then lose them roughly a third faster.A year in, only about one in five subscribers is still paying.The pattern is simple and a little embarrassing. People try the AI app, get their “wow,” and then just stop opening it, because, often, it was just a novelty experience. Venture firm Bessemer has started warning that even business AI tools are heading for the same cliff unless they get themselves embedded into something people already use every day.This is basically the same problem people had with Google+ (remember that?). Google got hundreds of millions of people to sign up, and then 90 percent of sessions lasted under five seconds.You can build a gorgeous destination, pour a fortune into it, and get everyone to sign up once, and it still dies if nobody comes back.Nir Eyal called what these app are missing the Hook Model, that products become habits through a loop of trigger, action, reward, and investment, each pass making the next one more likely. A novelty AI app nails the middle of that loop, you act, you get your clever reward, once, but there’s nothing pulling you back tomorrow and nothing that costs you to simply walk away from it. The loop never closes, so a habit never forms.On the enterprise side, the rejection is blunter and faster. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve heard large companies insist they are not taking on yet another tool. At this point, they often already have their own internal AI product and don’t want a new destination, a new login, a new thing for their people to remember to visit.They want the capability dropped inside the systems they already use, where the work already happens. Snyk, a security firm, studied more than 3,000 enterprise environments and found exactly that. Companies are stitching AI into their existing stack, not buying standalone products to use in parallel.This is bigger than a retention problem.The destination is dying. Not AI, AI is everywhere and growing. The app is dying.The idea that you deliver intelligence by building a place for people to come get it is over. The future is no app at all, intelligence woven invisibly into the tools people already live in, surfacing when it’s useful and getting out of the way when it isn’t.While that may sound clean, it isn’t. The same companies that want the AI invisible also want it completely under their control. They want it to disappear into the workflow and they want a dashboard, an audit trail, a record of every time it ran and what it touched.Invisible to the user, totally visible to the owner.Those two desires are at war, and whoever satisfies both at once is going to win the next decade of AI products.We need to take stock of why the app model is collapsing, what the people buying AI actually want instead, why “invisible” is so much harder than it sounds, and where the real work, and the real careers, are moving.The companies still pouring money into beautiful standalone AI apps are building tollbooths on a road people have already started to abandon.Google+ had hundreds of millions of accounts and almost no one who came back. A gorgeous destination nobody had a reason to visit twice.The app everyone downloaded and nobody keptSurprise, it’s not Quibi!Malika Aubakirova and Anjney Midha at a16z, working with OpenRouter, analyzed more than 100 trillion tokens of real-world AI usage. Stickiness, they found, doesn’t depend on your product’s interface or features, but rather on the capabilities of the underlying model.The same study found that fewer than one in ten weekly ChatGPT users ever bothers to try a competing assistant, despite there being zero cost to do it. People plant themselves in one big AI and stay.They will not leave ChatGPT. They will drop your ChatGPT wrapper in a week. Stickiness lives with the model and churn lives with the destination you built on it.People aren’t loyal to your app. They’re loyal to the intelligence inside it, and that intelligence is for rent, to everyone, including you.This is why the AI app graveyard is filling up so fast. Character.AI lost roughly 60 percent of its user base in a year.Jasper, one of the early AI-writing darlings, watched more than half its revenue evaporate.Google+ had hundreds of millions of accounts and almost no one who came back. A gorgeous destination nobody had a reason to visit twice.Yupp, an AI startup that raised thirty-three million dollars and signed up 1.3 million users, shut down anyway, with its founders explaining that the models underneath improved so fast that they never found a durable reason for anyone to keep coming back.Over a million people used the product and it still wasn’t a business..If that pattern feels familiar, it should. This is basically the MoviePass story with better branding (and I worked on MoviePass!).Millions signed up overnight. There was no durable business underneath, and it collapsed in a heap. A lot of AI apps are basically following this same model.MoviePass got millions of people to sign up almost overnight for something that felt like a cheat code, and the spectacular sign-up numbers meant nothing once it turned out there was no durable business underneath. Massive adoption, a value proposition that dissolved on contact with reality, and a collapse that happened faster than anyone expected.A lot of today’s AI apps are doing the exact same thing.Brian Balfour, the founder of Reforge and former head of growth at HubSpot, calls this “product-market fit collapse.” In normal software, customer expectations rise slowly, so a product that nails its market can coast for a while. In AI, he points out, expectations reset almost instantly.Every time a new model drops, users recalibrate what “good” even means, and dropping your app for whatever is newer, or for the raw model underneath it, costs them nothing. You are not building toward a stable finish line because the finish line keeps moving away from you every few months.We have a category with astonishing sign-up rates, near-zero switching costs, expectations that reset on a monthly basis, and no loyalty to anything except the model you don’t own.That same body of research points, almost accidentally, at the way out. The a16z study describes what it calls a “glass slipper” effect. When a user’s actual workflow fits a particular model so precisely that it creates real inertia, a cost, finally, to leaving. The apps that retain are the ones that have wedged themselves so deeply into something a person does every day that walking away would actually hurt.The answer is quite simple. Stop building a place for people to visit and start building something they can’t easily remove.Millions signed up overnight. There was no durable business underneath, and it collapsed in a heap. A lot of AI apps are running the same play with a nicer logo.What the people buying AI actually wantLarger companies say they aren’t adding another AI tool the way someone declines a second helping at a dinner they’re already full from. These are organizations that have spent two years drowning in AI pilots, logins, dashboards, and Chrome extensions, and they have hit a wall.Companies do not want another destination. They want the capability, the actual intelligence, dropped inside the systems their people already use, where the work already happens.The most striking version of it I’ve heard is that you shouldn’t even have to know you’re using a different product. You should just know that the thing you were doing got better.That is a remarkable thing for a company to say about a product it is paying for, and it is becoming the default expectation rather than the exception. The same instinct shows up outside the enterprise too. A news organization I talked with recently had no interest in building another app for people to download. They wanted their journalism to show up where people already are, in a text message, inside the AI assistant someone is already talking to, with no new place to go.This is where the measurable center of gravity has already moved, and the infrastructure numbers show it.The Model Context Protocol (MCP), the open standard that lets AI reach into the tools and data a company already uses, went from a developer curiosity to something closer to 97 million downloads a month and production use inside roughly 40 percent of technical organizations. Gartner expects that by the end of the 2026, 40 percent of enterprise applications will ship with task-specific AI agents built in.The designers paying attention have already clocked what this does to the job. Patrick Neeman puts it bluntly, that chat was only ever an interface, and agents are something else entirely.The design work, he argues, has moved to the contract underneath the product, the rules and handshakes that let one system quietly hand a task to another and get a trustworthy answer back. When the interface disappears, the thing you’re actually designing is the behavior.Think about what “invisible utility” has always looked like once a technology matures. Mark Weiser, the Xerox PARC scientist who coined the term “ubiquitous computing,” put it in a line that has aged remarkably well. “The most profound technologies are those that disappear. They weave themselves into the fabric of everyday life until they are indistinguishable from it.”Mark Weiser called it in 1991. “The most profound technologies are those that disappear.” He was describing the future of the interface before most of us had one. AI is finally proving him right.Nobody opens an app to use electricity. You don’t launch a program to get water out of the tap. The most important technologies succeeded precisely by disappearing, by becoming something simply present in the walls, available the instant you need it and invisible the rest of the time.That is the shape AI is racing toward, and the companies building beautiful standalone AI destinations are, in a sense, trying to sell you a generator and a trip to the well at the exact moment everyone else is wiring the building.The holy grail is a world where one AI simply calls another. Google’s Agent-to-Agent protocol, now governed by the Linux Foundation and adopted across more than 150 organizations, exists precisely so that one company’s AI can hand a task to a specialized capability elsewhere and get a usable answer back, with no human opening a separate product to make it happen.The interface vanishes completely into the workflow. It’s genuinely hard to build well, and the infrastructure is still young, but the direction is set. The companies that understand it are to disappear.That sounds like a potential answer. Make the intelligence invisible, embed it in the workflow, and, BOOM, you win. The problem is that the people who want it invisible want something else at the very same time, something that pulls in the exact opposite direction, and that contradiction is where most of this is going to get stuck.Enterprises want the AI invisible to their people and lit up like this for themselves, every action logged, every data path visible. Invisible to the user, accountable to the owner. Almost nobody has built both.Nobody has figured out invisible, but watchedThe answer seems to be to make AI invisible. Embed it, dissolve it into the workflow, let it work without anyone having to go anywhere. Simple.Except it isn’t, and the reason is entirely stuck in humanity. The same companies that demand the AI be invisible to their employees demand that it be completely visible to them.They want it to disappear into the workflow, and they want a dashboard showing every time it ran. They want it to act without being summoned, and they want an audit trail of everything it touched. They want it woven invisibly into the fabric of everyday life, to borrow Weiser’s phrase, and they want a kill switch they can reach in half a second, a demand that turns out to be mostly aspirational.In a Writer’s enterprise survey, more than a third of employees said they couldn’t immediately pull the plug on a rogue AI agent even if they needed to. Invisible to the user, yet totally visible to the owner.The same leaders who tell me they want our capability to vanish into their systems will, ten minutes later, ask how they’ll track exactly who used it, how often, and what it returned, so they can prove the ROI to their own bosses. One large company essentially wanted the product to be invisible to its workforce and fully instrumented for its executives at the same time.A recurring, hard stop in these conversations is data. More than one major brand has told me, flatly, that they will not feed their proprietary information into an outside tool, no matter how good it is, and that any vendor has to guarantee the model underneath isn’t quietly learning from what they put in.Invisible is fine. Ungoverned is a non-starter.Security researchers now treat this as table stakes.Becky Brooks describes how organizations need to be able to answer basic questions about every AI action, which tools it called, what data passed through, whether any of it was proprietary, and most of them can’t.The data behind that fear is genuinely alarming. The Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, the most-cited study in enterprise security, found that employee use of unapproved AI tools tripled in a single year, to 45 percent of the workforce, with two-thirds of those people using personal accounts outside any corporate control.Cyberhaven’s analysis found the average employee now feeds sensitive data into an AI tool about once every three days.IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach report found that a growing majority of breached companies had no governance in place to manage AI or even detect its unapproved use.The AI already has disappeared into the workflow.It gets starker when you look at the actual network traffic. Infrastructure company Kong examined enterprise AI usage running through its systems and found that fewer than 1 percent of organizations had any AI-specific governance controls in place.Meanwhile, almost 98 percent of their AI requests were flowing out to third-party proprietary services, every one of them carrying prompts, context, and often sensitive data outside the company’s own walls.OutSystems found 94 percent of organizations worried that AI sprawl is piling up complexity, technical debt, and security risk, while only around 12 percent have any centralized way to manage it. Everyone feels the car accelerating. Almost nobody has their hands on the wheel.There’s an old piece of political wisdom that fits this moment better than it has any right to. “Trust, but verify.” The companies buying AI have landed in exactly that posture, except the technology has made the two halves nearly impossible to hold at once.The whole appeal of invisible AI is that you don’t have to watch it. The whole fear of invisible AI is that you can’t.A thing designed to operate without your attention is, by definition, a thing operating outside your attention, and that is a terrifying property to hand a system that can touch your data, your customers, and your decisions.This is the actual product problem of the next decade. The winning AI products will be the ones that pull off the paradox of being genuinely invisible to the person doing the work, and genuinely transparent to the person who owns the risk.Disappear for the user. Light up like a control room for the owner. The teams that treat “invisible” as the whole goal are going to build things no serious company will deploy, because they solved for elegance and ignored accountability. The teams that bury everything in dashboards and approval gates will build something so visible and so clunky that it’s just another tool nobody opens, which puts us right back where we started.Enterprises want the AI invisible to their people and lit up like this for themselves: every action logged, every data path visible. Invisible to the user, accountable to the owner. Almost nobody has built both.Getting both right is brutally hard. It’s also the only version of this that actually wins.Enterprises want the AI invisible to their people and lit up like this for themselves, every action logged, every data path visible. Invisible to the user, accountable to the owner. Almost nobody has built both.Move Up the Stack or Get Buried in ItIf you design or build products for a living, this could read like a eulogy for your job. It isn’t. The app dying is not the same as the work dying.The work moved, and the people who notice where it went are going to be fine. The people who keep polishing the thing that’s going away are the ones who should be nervous.Nielsen Norman Group has been studying how people actually use software since before most AI founders could type, put it about as plainly as it can be put, AI didn’t kill UX, it moved where the value lives.The interface, the screen, the thing we used to spend all our time perfecting, is becoming a commodity. You can generate a competent one in an afternoon now. What you cannot generate in an afternoon is the judgment about what the system should do, when it should speak up, when it should stay quiet, what it’s allowed to touch, and how a human stays in control of something built to run without them.Patrick Neeman has a sharp way of framing the trap we have to design our way out of. The reason everyone reached for chat, he argues, is that conversation is good enough at standing in for everything that it can hide the real product rather than reveal it.The thing that feels like the answer, a text box you talk to, is often the thing keeping you from building what the moment actually needs.The designer’s job used to be drawing the screen. Now it’s deciding the behavior, the rules and handshakes underneath, the contract between systems that no user will ever see but every user will feel.The hardest, highest-value version of that work is the paradox from a minute ago, made real.Mangus Eriksen lands on the exact tension this whole piece has been circling. Invisible AI only works if people trust it, and trust requires transparency and real control, without burying that control three menus deep. Read that next to the governance data from earlier and you have the entire job description for the next decade of product work.Make it disappear for the person using it. Make it accountable to the person who owns it. Hide the machinery, surface the controls. That is a genuinely hard design problem, and it is nothing like designing a prettier chat window.Think about what happened to the switchboard operator. In the early 20th century, connecting phone calls by hand was one of the most common jobs for young women in America. Then AT&T automated it, and the economists James Feigenbaum and Daniel Gross documented what followed. Once a city switched to dial, the operator jobs didn’t shrink, they vanished, dropping 50 to 80 percent and never coming back.The need underneath, connecting people reliably, didn’t vanish at all. It moved up the stack, into switching systems and the engineers who design them, and it got more valuable. The part that matters is this: the women who were operators mostly didn’t make that jump.The function moved up, and a lot of the people defined by the old version of it got left behind. The ones who thrived were the ones who moved to the layer underneath before they were forced to.This connects to something that’s becoming ubiquitous in AI. Nobody is coming to hand you the next version of your job. Not in the broad economy, and not in our corner of it.The people who make it through every one of these shifts are the ones who stop defending the thing they were good at and start building the thing the new world actually needs, before they’re forced to. In this case, that means letting go of the beautiful destination and getting good at the invisible, accountable system underneath it.The future of AI is the intelligence woven so completely into the tools people already use that they stop noticing it’s there, with a clean pane of glass that lets whoever is responsible see exactly what it’s doing. Invisible to the user. Accountable to the owner. Almost nobody is building for both yet, which is precisely why it’s the opportunity.The companies still pouring money into gorgeous standalone AI apps are building elegant tollbooths on a road people have already started to leave. The winners are somewhere else entirely, down in the plumbing, making the intelligence disappear into the work and handing the owner the keys to watch it.The destination is dead. The infrastructure is where everything now lives.References and further readingWhy the app model is collapsingMalika Aubakirova, Anjney Midha, Alex Atallah, Chris Clark, Justin Summerville, State of AI: An Empirical 100 Trillion Token Study. item.title: What I told the CFO when he asked why design matters
item.description: How to sell design and show the impact of design outcomes to business and finance leaders.Many years ago a business unit CFO told me: “I don’t need another presentation explaining why design is important. I need to know whether investing another million dollars in design will outperform investing it in engineering or marketing.”That conversation changed how I talk about design. Showing the value of design with quantitative data is one of the greatest challenges for a design leader. Our field has been a C-suite priority for years, but it’s still treated as a secondary contributor to business performance.And part of that is on us. Many of us think of ourselves as artists of digital businesses, creative outsiders in conversations where everyone else talks numbers.That may be true, but it sounds too convenient. We design products, so we have to lead with business outcomes: know our numbers, sell our ideas, and quantify the real-world impact of what we do.If your CFO asked why design matters and what the value of your work is, what would you say?Here are the five answers I gave mine.#1. “Hold design to the same standard as any other investment: payback period and rate of return”Every request that crosses a CFO’s desk gets the same two questions: how fast does the money come back, and how much value will it create beyond that? Finance calls them the payback period and the rate of return, and it applies them to every investment (machinery, software, headcount…).My answer to that CFO was to judge design with those same two questions. Before giving him that answer, I had done my research and looked at real-world cases. In 2025, Forrester studied six global companies for the research platform UserTesting and tallied how much they spent on user research versus what they got in return.The design work is right there in the findings: validating designs with users before launching shortened iteration cycles by 25% and avoided $2.5 million in developer rework. The overall ROI was 415% over three years, and the spending paid for itself in less than six months. Most investments a CFO approves take years to do that.That study confirmed something I now repeat to every design leader I meet: finance already has the tools to evaluate design fairly, because it evaluates everything as an investment. We just have to hand over our numbers in that format.When designers can clearly show the value of their work, it’s hard to question the budget, and that’s when you get the opportunity to try more ambitious work. Measured wins buy credibility.#2. “Conversion is revenue we’ve already paid to acquire”Companies know to the cent what they pay to bring a visitor in: marketing audits every campaign, every channel and every cost-per-click (CPC, CPA, cost per lead…). All of that money is spent by the time someone loads a shopping cart.What happens after the click is, in most cases, considered the designer’s job and treated as a cosmetic layer. It’s hard to connect it to money. However, there’s data that proves it’s more tied to revenue than it seems.The numbers I sometimes use to make this case come from Baymard Institute, which has calculated that seven out of ten shopping carts die at checkout (an average of 70.22%).In many cases, this issue can be solved through design changes. According to their research, large e-commerce sites can lift conversion by 35.26% if they fix known checkout design issues. They estimate $260 billion in lost orders is recoverable in the US and EU through those fixes alone!Every time I’ve presented these numbers to a non-design audience, the reaction has been the same: nobody had ever counted checkout friction as lost revenue. The money was always there, but it had no owner.That’s why conversion is where I tell design leaders to start if they’ve never connected design to revenue. The attribution is clean, the results show fast, and finance tracks the metric for you.#3. “User research is capital protection”Every product idea can be tested before it’s built by making a prototype. You put it in front of a certain number of users, and within a few weeks you know whether the idea works. Total cost: one designer’s time.Or you can skip the test, spend months building the product with several teams, and find out at launch that the idea didn’t work.That’s what validation is for. When a test kills a bad idea early, the company saves everything it would have spent building it. Those savings never appear in reports, because nobody documents the disasters that didn’t happen. That’s why research always looks like the easiest thing to cut when budgets get tight, which is precisely why cutting research often proves expensive later.If you need external proof, I recommend you read McKinsey’s Business Value of Design study. In this report, McKinsey tracked 300 companies over five years. The top performers grew revenue 32 percentage points faster and returned 56 percentage points more to shareholders (share price gains plus dividends) than their industry peers. One of the practices those companies shared was continually testing and iterating with users during development.Validating pays twice: less money wasted on bad ideas, better products when the idea is good. These days I pitch it as ‘capital protection’ instead of research. Same work, faster approval.#4. “A design system compounds like capital: build once, deploy everywhere”Every quarter, I have a sense of the hours my teams saved by reusing components and UX patterns, translated into cost savings. It’s the design number finance verifies fastest, because it’s included in the timesheets and payroll data they trust.That habit exists thanks to our design system: the library of components (buttons, forms, menus…), patterns and reusable experiences, that teams design and code once and then reuse everywhere. Those pieces are one of design’s few compounding assets. You pay for them once, and they keep paying back every time someone reuses them.If you don’t have your own numbers yet, Sparkbox has public ones. In a small, controlled experiment, eight developers built the same page twice: first from scratch, then using an open-source design system. The scratch version took a median of 4.2 hours; with the design system, they built it in 2 hours.Scale those hours across everything a product team ships in a year and the savings add up to weeks of work. With consistent components, there’s less quality assurance. and fewer support tickets. New designers can ship sooner because the pieces they use are there from day one.Any team running a design system can pull the same numbers from its own tools.#5. “When features become commodities, design is the pricing power”Today, any feature we ship can be copied by a competitor within weeks. AI accelerated this for everyone. The AI in Design Report 2026 (a survey of 906 designers in 60+ countries) found that 91% of designers now use AI at least weekly, up from 54% the year before.When every team builds with the same tools, products end up with similar features. And when two products do the same thing, people choose the one that’s easier and nicer to use. Customers are often willing to pay more for that experience and remain loyal longer. Finance has a name for being able to charge more without losing customers: pricing power.Experience has become the differentiator and one of the main reasons a customer would choose your product over competitors’. It’s what protects the price. The responsibility of building an outstanding user experience is, of course, on designers.There’s measurable financial impact behind our craftNone of the five answers I’ve shared in this article required inventing new math. Payback, conversion, validation, reuse and pricing power are terms your CFO uses daily.If you lead a design team, your job is to translate what you do into terms and numbers your finance team can understand and validate.Two habits have helped me. The first is to talk to finance before you need something from them. Ask what they report every month and which numbers they argue over, because that’s the fastest crash course in how your company measures itself. The second is to report design metrics on a schedule. You’ll build more trust with your C Suite if you present your team’s performance, in business terms, periodically. It shows you understand that design, like every other function, answers for its results.One thing I always clarify in these conversations is that money is only half of the design’s value. Besides the monetary value (productivity, fewer user errors, lower training and support costs), there is also human value (user satisfaction, inclusion, customer loyalty, adoption).I’ve never had a CFO reject the human half when it came with the monetary one.As for being ‘the artists of digital businesses’: We can keep the craft and speak numbers at the same time. In my experience, that combination is what gets design taken seriously.Arin Bhowmick (@arinbhowmick) is Chief Design Officer at SAP, based in San Francisco, California. item.title: Taste is not a design methodology
item.description: Judgment brings the facts. Agency puts them on the table. AI assisted.It has become our favorite answer to AI-generated sameness. The reality is good products come from judgment built on facts, and the agency to use them when the room prefers opinions.Ask Rick Rubin what he does and he’ll tell you he has “no technical ability” and knows nothing about music. In a 2023 interview with Anderson Cooper, the producer said artists pay him for confidence in his own taste.https://medium.com/media/1f83a53654c7bc936b099303acddda54/href“The confidence I have in my taste and my ability to express what I feel has proven helpful for artists.” — Rick RubinEveryone now wants that job.Just typing this makes me squirm because I believe the field should be research and data driven as much as it can be. With humans even.“Taste is the new moat” might be the industry’s favorite sentence of 2026: artificial intelligence made competent screens cheap, so the one thing left to sell is the judgment to pick the good one. A ProductLed interview in January went further, telling builders not to validate before they build. It’s about 45 minutes in.I decided not to show the video inline because it adds fuel to the fire and their use of typography isn’t to my taste.It’s come up with couple of authors I follow — The taste paradox by Nicole Alexandra Michaelis is a good read over at UX Collective, and Xinran Ma had a interview recently about it in UX — and it’s in the zeitgeist.My point is that it’s the wrong word.Maybe it plays out like this. I hope not.The moat crowd is right that judgment matters; they’re wrong about where it comes from:Taste is a preference. It comes from what you’ve seen and who you admire, and two people with different taste can disagree with no way to settle it.Judgment is a claim you can check. It rests on principles research has tested, plus evidence about your users, so it can be explained, taught, and shown wrong.Judgment needs agency too, because someone has to raise those facts when the most senior voice would rather trade opinions. What Nicole Alexandra Michaelis and Xinran Ma are talking about Judgement i.e. experience they can back with facts and experience.The short rule: if you can’t name the fact or research behind a call, it’s still an opinion, which is otherwise known as taste.Admit taste is an opinionIn 2001, researchers in Bordeaux and Montpellier gave a panel of 54 tasters a white wine colored red with an odorless dye. The panel described it with the vocabulary of red wine.Nothing had changed but the color, and that was enough to overwrite their noses.That’s the trouble with treating taste as a standard: it’s an opinion that feels like a fact. Two skilled designers can look at the same screen, reach opposite conclusions, and neither can prove the other mistaken.Taste feels like perception, but a lot of it is expectation. Apple Music is probably the best example, it’s Apple, but still a challenging application to use established as fact.My beautiful car, and not for everyone. A taste call, for sure.For example, I like driving Audi TTs. A lot.The proportions, the way one sits on a highway on-ramp, the complete impracticality of the back seat, the beautifully designed cockpit, the race to 110 miles per hour in California.That last part is just storytelling, really.I don’t expect any of that to be anyone else’s taste, and nothing is wrong when it isn’t, because my taste in cars only has to satisfy only me. A product has to work for thousands of people who never met me for it to be profitable, and that’s where a preference stops being enough.My expectation is that Audi TT’s are designed for my taste, and it doesn’t fail me, ever.Design has its own version of the wine study.In 1995, Masaaki Kurosu and Kaori Kashimura of Hitachi had people rate 26 ATM layouts and found that how usable a layout looked tracked its beauty far more than its inherent usability. The field now calls this the aesthetic-usability effect, and it cuts both ways.Generative tools make this worse because they turn out polished screens by default, so every option in the review looks finished. That’s the blind spot in the moat argument: the less polish costs, the less polish can tell you.A just above average table generated by Lovable.It reminds me of a conversation I had with Scott Jenson — Generative AI makes a lot of beautifully just above average screens. I made that argument they’re still better than a lot of portfolios I have seen, even if the screens have less depth.This is why “does it have taste?” makes a weak review question: it has no failure condition other than an opinion.Ruiqi Zhou called taste unfalsifiable in a February essay named Taste Is the New Moat — And That’s the Problem. It’s a great read, and points out that a standard you can never fail works more like a status marker, and status markers reward whoever already holds status. Usually, that’s product management.Build judgment on laws that have held for centuriesUser experience borrowed its foundations from people who ran experiments, and they had computers in only some cases.Paul Fitts, Dieter Rams and Jakob Nielsen at a conference that exists only in AI.Here are examples:Paul Fitts showed in 1954 that the time to hit a target depends on its size and distance using fighter cockpits for research, and William Edmund Hick showed that decision time climbs as options pile up. Both findings have held up for seven decades.Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich developed heuristic evaluation in 1990, and the ten heuristics are still the default checklist. Each turns an opinion into a checkable claim, like a button too small for a thumb.Dieter Rams and his ten principles took what could have stayed personal taste and wrote it down where other people could use it, which is why teams still audit work against them fifty years on.They are normative rather than experimental, but a checklist can be argued with. I keep plain-language summaries of Fitts’s Law, Hick’s Law, Nielsen’s heuristics, and Rams’s principles on ux-guidelines.com, a reference site I maintain. Every law has conditions, and knowing them is part of judgment.Hick’s Law describes a choice among equally likely options, and a 1985 study of its exceptions found cases where adding choices barely slowed people down. Fitts measured people tapping a stylus between two targets, not a thumb stretching across a phone.A law applied outside its conditions is just another opinion with a citation.Principles don’t settle everything.At Microsoft, Ronny Kohavi’s team reported that only about a third of well-run experiments improved the metric they were designed to move. The laws tell you what’s likely, and testing tells you what happened.User research earns its place next to the laws for the same reason.The golden ratio. 300 BC. That’s before the iPhone, kids, but it doesn’t work for everything, by design.A law is general and your users are specific, so only watching them shows which steps they repeat and where they give up. Teresa Torres makes the cadence the point, defining continuous discovery as weekly contact with customers by the team building the product, rather than a study that lands after the decision.Test beauty with the people who will use itNone of this means beauty is decoration. The same aesthetic-usability effect explains why users forgive attractive products, and appearance shapes trust and first impressions.Don Norman gave the effect a mechanism in Emotional Design: a positive mood broadens thinking and makes people more forgiving of small friction. Jony Ive’s teams built the most admired hardware of their era and also shipped the butterfly keyboard, which Apple settled a class action over for $50 million in 2022 after years of complaints.Taste operating at that altitude still needed someone to check whether the thing worked.The average attractiveness rating for each screenshot for both young adults and older adults ( 1 = unattractive, 7 = attractive)The mistake is assuming the designer’s eye can stand in for the audience’s. Nielsen Norman Group showed the same five screenshots to 229 adults aged 18 to 25 and 228 aged 35 and older,The results?The younger group rated the flat designs slightly more attractive.The older, slightly less attractive.Whose taste was right? Each group’s, for itself.Beauty is in the eye of the beholder, especially in enterprise software, where the person who admires the demo is rarely the one who lives in the product eight hours a day.Beauty is a user outcome, so measure it like one.That’s where the line between fact and opinion falls here. What users report about a screen is a fact about your audience, while a design lead’s verdict is one more opinion, however practiced the eye behind it. The survey used a modified version of the Microsoft Desirability Toolkit, which asks people to pick words that describe what they see from a fixed list.Score task success and time on task separately from those ratings, so a polished prototype can’t inflate the verdict on whether the thing works.Teach the principles before the portfolioIn 2009, two researchers who had spent careers on opposite sides of this argument wrote a paper together. Daniel Kahneman had documented how judgment fails, while Gary Klein had defended expert intuition in the field.Their joint answer on when intuition deserves trust came down to two conditions:The environment has to be regular enough to learn about who they’re designing forThe person needs a real chance to learn itDesign taste rarely gets that chance. A designer ships a screen, moves on to the next project, and never finds out whether the choice helped anyone.Confidence grows with years, but accuracy only grows with feedback.Tell a designer two years out of school to trust their taste, after a portfolio course, maybe an internship, and very few closed loops between a decision and its outcome. What they have is exposure to showcase sites and admired apps, which produces taste that matches the feed, not the user.Principles are the shortcut experience can’t hand out, and they come with standing. A junior designer who knows Hick’s Law can push back on a longer menu in her first critique, and a new hire who has studied the heuristics can flag a missing undo before anyone senior does.Facts give people the agency that seniority usually keeps for itself.Give everyone the agency to argue from factsTaste has a politics problem.When the standard is taste, the taste that counts usually belongs to the most senior person present. Ron Kohavi named it in a 2008 Stanford talk, Listen to Your Customers not to the HiPPO: the HiPPO is the highest-paid person’s opinion.A taste culture is a HiPPO culture with better typography.Thank you, Productboard.The fix isn’t to ban taste from the room, it’s to stop one person from owning it without evidence.Everybody on a team has taste, and the new designer’s is worth as much as the vice president’s, which is exactly why it makes a poor standard: nothing decides whose version wins except rank. Facts don’t work that way, since a law or a session recording says the same thing no matter who reads it out.Taste cultures have a patron saint they misappropriated: Steve Jobs.He told BusinessWeek in 1998 that designing by focus group is hard. People, he said, “don’t know what they want until you show it to them.” It gets quoted as permission to skip research, though the same answer described watching trends and studying Apple’s installed base.Paul Rand and Steve Jobs in an AI collaboration.But even he met his match in Paul Rand.When Steve Jobs needed a logo for NeXT in 1986, he hired Rand, whom he openly called the greatest living graphic designer. The friction came immediately: Jobs asked for a few options, and Rand refused, saying he would solve the problem and Jobs would pay him, and if he wanted options he could hire someone else.This is what you get when you hire the best logo designer of all time. Steve Jobs learned a lot from this exercise.Jobs agreed to the terms and the $100,000 fee. Rand returned with one design, the tilted black cube, presented in a hand-bound booklet that walked Jobs through the reasoning until the logo felt inevitable.Jobs loved it, and later admitted that you don’t hand a genius a menu.Because of this, Apple did research all the time and that gave Jobs credibility to make judgement calls. Those that claim they have the same truly understand the company, nor how to combine taste with judgement.2x2 Matrix Strategy. Simplicity in action.Even Steve Jobs’ famous 2x2 Matrix Strategy is rooted in science — Paradox of Choice.The larger problem is survivorship bias, another old law. We remember the founder whose certainty paid off and forget the rooms where the same certainty sank the product with dollar amount attached to it.Agency with receipts is the fix.Session notes, retention data, and a heuristic all lose to a senior “that feels off,” unless the team agrees that facts outrank opinions.With that agreement in place, the quietest person in the room can win by naming the law a design breaks or the data point it ignores. Peter Merholz argues that design executives earn that standing by making design their secondary concern.41 Shades of Blue comes with a dollar amount.The fair counterargument belongs to Doug Bowman, Google’s first visual designer.In 2009 he left and explained why in Goodbye, Google: a team was testing 41 shades of blue, and he had been asked to prove whether a border should be three, four, or five pixels wide.His complaint went past the trivia: with nobody senior who understood design, he argued, the company ran out of reasons for its decisions, and data became “a crutch for every decision” that kept anything daring from shipping.$200 million later. Hard to argue that as an outcome.Measuring everything is its own way of dodging judgment, so decisions slow to the test calendar, and designers who could settle a border width from a principle leave for places where that counts, as Bowman did.Aim evidence at the choices that change what users can do. A corner radius needs no significance test, since a law settles it faster.Choose facts over opinionsJudgment is knowing which facts apply, and where they stop applying: a law, a heuristic, a published study, or research on your own users. Where taste says “this feels right,” judgment points out that the target is too small to tap reliably and that Fitts showed why in 1954.Agency is saying that out loud in the review, even when it cuts against the most senior opinion in the room.Judgment tells you which facts matter, and agency is using them when the room prefers an opinion.The new reality:Generative tools can produce fifty layouts before my morning coffee.Judgment cuts the pile fast, dropping the ones with targets too small to hit, menus too long to scan, and flows that ask people to hold too much in their heads.What’s left goes to research, where users settle what the principles can’t.Teams that run interviews and usability sessions on a schedule build a store of facts they can reach for in any review, and teams that skip them are left with preferences and a deadline. Dan Maccarone spent a year rebuilding his studio’s process around these tools and found that it didn’t make the work faster, which he counts as the point: what changed was where the thinking had to happen.Rubin’s approach works because a record has no task to fail. A designer who borrows that job description claims the authority without the conditions that make it hold.Judgment also improves in a way taste doesn’t, if somebody writes the call down. Jeff Gothelf formalizes that in the Lean UX canvas: state what you believe will happen, then name the evidence that would tell you whether you were right. It’s the equivalent of the Change My Mind meme, and it’s brilliant.Picture two designers.One moves a filter panel above the results because Hick’s Law favors fewer competing choices on the way to what people came for, predicts lower search abandonment, and checks the numbers six weeks after launch.The other spends the same six weeks studying award-winning screen shots.Only the first one learned something new about their users, and only their judgment got sharper.ConclusionTaste isn’t going away, and it isn’t the real enemy.Opinions shape style, brand voice, and the small choices no principle covers. The trouble starts when an opinion gets treated as a fact and wins arguments it hasn’t earned.The moat story is half right.Artificial intelligence does make average output cheap, and plenty of products will look alike because of it. The scarce skill isn’t picking the prettiest variation, it’s knowing which ones break what the field already knows, which ones deserve a test, and what the result means for the next decision.The wine panel in Bordeaux wasn’t foolish; its members were human, and so are we. That’s the whole reason design has laws and methods at all.Human perception drifts toward what it expects to see, and principles are how a field keeps itself honest across decades of new tools.So learn the laws, read the research carefully, and give your team the agency to use both. Then let your users decide the rest. Judgment you can explain, backed by the nerve to raise it, will outlast taste you can only defend, and teams built on it will ship the products everyone else ends up copying.Action ItemsAsk “what fact supports this?” instead of “does it have taste?” In critiques, every significant call should rest on a principle, a study, or something your users did. If nobody can name one, label the call an opinion and flag it for testing.Teach the laws before the look. Give junior designers Fitts’s Law, Hick’s Law, cognitive load theory, and Nielsen’s heuristics before mood boards. Principles hand them decades of feedback, and the standing to use it.Make it safe to push back with facts. Say plainly that a cited principle or data point outranks a job title, and back the junior designer who uses one against you. Agency that gets punished once rarely shows up twice.Test where the facts run out. Brand feel, new interaction patterns, and cases where two laws conflict all need research. Run a usability session, a few interviews, or a first-click test that week, and log the prediction behind it. Leave the border widths alone.Taste is not a design methodology was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: The synth everyone owned and few could program: a lesson for AI design
item.description: AI made quality available to everyone, and made it average. What sets work apart now is a decision you can see.An AI assistant helped me write this. The ideas, the data and the final edit are mine.E.PIANO 1In 1983, Yamaha released the DX7, the first digital synthesizer to sell in large numbers. It was powerful and almost impossible to program: no knobs to shape the sound, only menus on a small display that few musicians ever learned to navigate. So it shipped with factory sounds, 128 presets that two specialists had put together in less than four days. Most owners never went further.The Yamaha DX7 (1983): a membrane panel, a small display and no knobs. Photo: iixorbiusii, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).One of those sounds, “E.PIANO 1”, imitates an electric piano. It sounds professional from the first note. The music theorist Megan Lavengood counted how often it shows up on the charts: in 1986, it is on 39% of the Billboard Hot 100 number ones, 40% of the country number ones and 61% of the R&B number ones. Her study is called “What makes it sound ‘80s?”: a quality sound handed to everyone became the signature of a decade, and then the surest way to date a record.The same year, Brian Eno released Apollo with Daniel Lanois and his brother Roger, an ambient album written for a documentary about the Moon missions, and he used the DX7 on it. He was one of the few people who could program the machine in depth. Yet his case reads as a matter of order more than technique: music imagined for those images first, then the sounds to make it, which no preset contained.The 2026 presetGenerative AI is doing to design what the DX7 did to sound. It gives a clean result to someone who doesn’t know how to adjust the tool, and that result converges.I measured it on twelve app briefs, with seven models from three makers (results and public benchmark). For a corporate law firm, all seven pick navy blue with a touch of gold. The average gap between their colours is only 9, the same as for a funeral home, measured in ΔE, the distance between two colours as the eye perceives it: under 10, they are shades of the same colour. The category sets the look.Home screens coded by five models for two of the briefs, in a pilot run of the benchmark. Image: author’s benchmark; people’s names blurred.The primary colour chosen by seven AI models for six app briefs. On the right, the average difference (ΔE): under 10, they are shades of the same colour. Image: author’s benchmark.Prose is going the same way. In a 2024 study published in Science Advances, Anil Doshi and Oliver Hauser had people write short stories with or without ideas from a language model. With the help, stories were rated more creative and better written, especially among the less confident writers. They were also more similar to one another, what researchers call homogenization. In another field, selection decisions such as hiring, the computer scientists Jon Kleinberg and Manish Raghavan described a related effect in 2021, algorithmic monoculture: when everyone relies on the same algorithm, each of them can come out ahead while the group as a whole does worse.The DX7 preset had at least been chosen, once, by two people, for no song in particular. The AI’s preset was chosen by nobody: it’s an average. What you recognize in a screen or a paragraph that looks AI-made is something nobody chose.The preset looks goodPresets didn’t wait for models. In 2013, Paul Adams, then VP of Product at Intercom, was already warning against the Dribbblisation of design: interfaces polished for the shot rather than for the problem.What’s new is elsewhere. For a long time, the preset showed: a template looked like a template, and moving away from it bought visible quality. The 2026 preset shows much less. It is coherent and polished on the surface, sometimes more finished than what a small team in a hurry would have shipped. As Tanya Donska put it in Built In: “All of it is correct. All of it could belong to anything.” Not all of it is correct, though: in the same measurement, 34 primary colours out of 84 fail the minimum contrast for white text on top, which you only see once you check.The 34 primary colours that fail with white text on top, shown as buttons with their contrast ratio (WCAG minimum: 4.5:1). The models set no label colour, so white is the case tested. Image: author’s benchmark.So apparent quality has become the floor. Much of the value people saw in designers came from the gap between ordinary work and careful work, and the machine now closes that gap on demand. Whatever sets work apart has moved somewhere else.Three ways out, and only one holdsThe first idea is to do better than the machine. Two things need separating here. Fixing what it gets wrong, like that contrast, is still essential, but it’s verification: an audit tool flags it just as well, and it sets no one apart. What holds up badly is the race for finish, because the floor rises with every new model and this year’s extra polish will be next year’s average.The second is to be original. It doesn’t hold up either, and the same data shows why. I asked the same models to avoid clichés. They did drop Playfair Display and Bebas Neue, but two-thirds of their new headings landed on a new repertoire, with Fraunces 19 times out of 84 and Space Grotesk 15 times. Originality pursued as a goal ends up averaged in turn, just a little later.Most frequent heading fonts in 84 designs, with the plain prompt and with “avoid clichés”. Image: author’s benchmark.That leaves decisions. A decision differs from an instruction by its content: “avoid clichés” says nothing about the product, while a decision starts from what this particular product has, which the average doesn’t know. And it has to be held. The boxing gym brief said “a boxing gym in a working-class neighbourhood of Marseille, members are mostly young adults who train hard.” The seven models still returned roughly the same thing: bright red or orange on a near-black background, with condensed headings for six of them. To describe the mood they were going for, they chose words like “raw, intense, gritty”, with no trace of Marseille or of the neighbourhood, as if the category had covered up the context in the brief. Deciding, then, means defending what’s particular against the pull of the category, at every step where the preset comes back.The boxing gym brief: background, primary colour and heading font chosen by seven models, with their mood words. “Train hard” is sample text; none of the answers mentions Marseille. Image: author’s benchmark.“It looks AI”This changes the design review. “It looks AI” has become a common remark, about a mockup as much as a text. It sounds like a comment on quality, and it often works as an accusation.The daycare brief, coded by five models from three makers in a pilot run of the benchmark. Four mention a Sarah, three name the app after a sprout, three have a Butterfly Room, and four show the 9:41 status bar of a marketing screenshot. Image: author’s benchmark.Yet the look it points to doesn’t prove that a machine was involved. A person following the defaults produces the same thing, and a model given real decisions, a colour with its reason or a constraint specific to the product, can move away from it. The look only proves that the preset stayed. Treating it as evidence turns the review into a trial: people ask who made the screen, and nobody discusses what it should be.The remark has a useful version, which is to name the preset. Maya Brennan’s guide to de-slopifying designs is a good list of what to name. This gradient came with the tool: what should our colour say here? This card grid is the standard layout: what does this content actually need? Put that way, the question asks for a decision, and it applies just as much to a screen drawn by hand. As hipuku writes, with generative tools “the first version turns up before the opinion has formed”. Naming the preset reopens that frame.For a team, that comes down to two habits. In review, ask what came from the preset before judging whether it works. In the design system, write the reason for each choice next to its value. An entry that reads “primary colour: #1B2A4A” says nothing more than the preset. “Primary colour: the blue of the firm’s original sign, darkened to hold contrast” shows a decision, and gives the next person a reason to keep it or change it.The same design system entry, without and with its reason. Diagram: author.A common objection is that you just need to give the AI a design system. That is indeed the right answer, as long as someone has made the decisions it contains.The question to keepE.PIANO 1 sounded great in 1986, which is exactly why it ended up everywhere, before it dated every record that kept it as it was. The 2026 look will probably go the same way. The preset was never a quality problem, and once quality is a given, only one question is left to ask in front of a screen: did someone decide this?Cover photo: Leo-setä, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0), cropped.Mathieu Poli is Head of Frontend Engineering at GoodBarber and writes about frontend engineering, product design and AI.The synth everyone owned and few could program: a lesson for AI design was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: What are we willing to sacrifice for AI?
item.description: Three paths forward, each challenging what we value most.Photo by Josh Johnson on UnsplashI suspect artificial intelligence may eventually accomplish what generations of socialists have struggled to achieve. And the irony is that capitalism may ultimately be responsible for making it happen.What makes this possibility particularly uncomfortable for me is that my political instincts lean libertarian. I have never been particularly enthusiastic about government-supplemented incomes, wealth redistribution, or expanding the state’s role in economic life.Yet the more I consider the potential consequences of AI-driven automation and its displacement of human labor, the more I recognize that a greater degree of centralized collective support may be necessary for society to continue to prosper.The economic arrangements I have long defended, particularly free markets and the principle of individual economic independence, may become difficult to sustain—not because their underlying principles have been disproven, but because the technology we are developing could fundamentally change the conditions upon which they depend.AI itself does not decide who benefits from its capabilities or who bears the costs. People do, through choices shaped by ambition, self-interest, competition, and greed. We may build machines capable of extraordinary intellectual achievements without becoming any wiser about the desires that govern their use. Those human incentives complicate every path forward.We appear to be heading toward a future in which artificial intelligence allows companies to produce much of what we need with a fraction of today’s workforce. Previous technological revolutions displaced workers but also created new occupations, and if you’re feeling optimistic, AI may do the same.But that optimism rests on the assumption that AI will follow a familiar historical pattern. Unlike previous technologies that automated particular forms of work, AI can perform an expanding range of intellectual tasks across industries, including some of the very capabilities people have historically relied upon to adapt to technological change.What happens to an economic system built around the relationship between work and income when fewer people are needed to produce the goods and services society consumes? And more interestingly, what happens to our philosophical convictions when the conditions that once justified them fundamentally change?As I see it, such a future points toward three broad directions, each requiring us to sacrifice one value in pursuit of another. Of course, some would argue that compromises are possible between the scenarios I’m about to present. Yet I question whether such compromises would offer more than temporary relief from the underlying tensions.The First Path: Sacrifice Profits to Preserve JobsThe first path forward would require businesses to sacrifice the additional profits AI could generate in order to preserve human employment and the economy built around it. This would not necessarily mean accepting losses or abandoning profitability, but rather voluntarily forgoing opportunities to earn more by replacing workers with AI. Companies would need to exercise restraint, even when doing so puts them at a competitive disadvantage.The problem is that businesses have powerful incentives to maximize profits, often by reducing costs and improving efficiency. As AI becomes more capable, replacing human workers becomes an attractive way to accomplish both, particularly when competitors are doing the same. Yet workers are also customers, and if enough people lose their jobs, businesses could eventually undermine the consumer economy that supports their profits.This is not simply a question of corporate greed, although in many cases it is. Some companies pursue greater profits, while others must reduce costs to remain competitive or survive. But companies are ultimately run by people, and the pursuit of wealth and power is as old as civilization itself.Greed has been recognized as a moral failing for centuries, yet that recognition has done little to eliminate it from human behavior. Expecting business leaders to collectively resist opportunities for greater wealth, particularly when their competitors have every incentive to pursue them, strikes me as wishful thinking.Sure, governments could attempt to impose such restraint through regulations, financial penalties, or incentives to retain workers. But businesses have spent generations minimizing taxes, relocating operations, lobbying lawmakers, and finding ways around regulations. Ultimately, such measures would do little to change the underlying incentive driving these decisions, as businesses will continue to seek opportunities to increase profits, even when doing so comes at the expense of human employment.The Second Path: Turn Away from AIRather than continuing down our current path, relying on businesses to restrain their pursuit of profits, or implementing targeted government regulations that may prove difficult to enforce, we could take a far more drastic approach and severely restrict the development and use of AI altogether. The objective would be to preserve the jobs on which economic independence currently depends.I understand the appeal of protecting people’s ability to support themselves through their own work, but consider what such a decision could cost us. AI might accelerate cancer research, develop more sustainable ways of producing food and energy, expand access to knowledge, and help solve problems that have resisted us for generations. I find it difficult to justify sacrificing those possibilities simply to preserve the way we currently earn a living.The difficulty is that there is no obvious way to separate acceptable uses of AI from unacceptable ones. We might welcome a system that advances scientific research while objecting when the same capabilities replace analysts, administrators, or other workers.Progress in one field can also disrupt employment in another. Someone would have to decide which benefits justify that disruption, which jobs deserve protection, and how much innovation society should forgo. Even if we agreed on those judgments today, new applications would make those boundaries harder to maintain tomorrow.There is also the question of whether such restrictions could endure. The impulse to invent, explore, and overcome limitations is as much a part of human nature as the pursuit of wealth or status. Nations, businesses, and research institutions would have powerful incentives to continue developing AI, particularly if their competitors were doing so. This path might preserve familiar forms of employment, but it would also require us to deliberately constrain a technology whose greatest benefits we have yet to discover.The Third Path: Reconsider What Liberty RequiresThat leaves the possibility I find most uncomfortable. We continue developing AI, accept that substantial labor displacement may occur, and reconsider how people obtain the resources necessary to live. Some form of guaranteed income, broader ownership of productive technology, or another mechanism may be required.I recognize that not every form of income support constitutes socialism, and I do not claim to know which approach would work best. But the deeper question is philosophical, not merely political. An economy built around the expectation that people earn their own living may have to confront a future in which opportunities to do so become increasingly scarce through no failure of individual effort.My instinct is to resist any arrangement that makes people more dependent on government. Yet the freedom to support oneself presupposes a meaningful opportunity to do so. Keynes imagined technological progress relieving humanity of much of its economic burden. We may achieve something resembling that ambition while retaining an economic system that requires most people to sell their labor to survive. We could make work less necessary without making workers any less dependent on having work.Considering greater economic intervention does not mean that replacing corporate power with government authority eliminates the human appetite for wealth, power, and control. Governments are no more immune to corruption than corporations, regardless of the virtues their political ideologies claim to represent. Changing the institutions that distribute resources does not change the human beings who operate them.My instincts are closer to subsidiarity, the principle that individuals and smaller communities should address problems within their capacity, with larger institutions stepping in when necessary. That could mean exploring local cooperatives that own AI tools, community land trusts, or regional funds that share the gains from automation rather than assuming any response must come from a central government. I want people to retain as much freedom and responsibility over their lives as possible.But if the means of earning a living become unavailable to large numbers of people, the problem may exceed what individuals or local communities can solve. Accepting that possibility would not require me to abandon liberty as a value. It would require me to question whether the institutions I have preferred can still protect it.Of course, new occupations may emerge, and the scale of displacement remains uncertain. Yet I believe AI has the potential to fundamentally disrupt the relationship between human labor and economic independence. Whether that disruption unfolds as dramatically as I have suggested remains to be seen, but the possibility alone forces me to reconsider economic and political convictions I have long held.What Are We Willing to Surrender?The first path asks businesses to sacrifice potential profits to preserve employment. The second asks us to restrain our impulse to invent and discover. The third asks us to reconsider how much institutional dependence we are willing to accept in order to preserve economic independence. Each presents a different kind of sacrifice, raising difficult questions about what we value and what we are willing to give up.I remain hopeful about what AI could make possible, and deeply uneasy about the society we might build around it. I have no desire to surrender my belief in individual liberty, but I am beginning to question whether the economic arrangements I have long defended will remain capable of protecting it. Perhaps the real test of our convictions is whether we can recognize when the means we have chosen no longer serve the ends we value.Don’t miss out!
